blocks.text: Meanwhile, lest you be surprised that the interpreters went different ways in explaining this word, here is another similar example in the word חטפיתא, by which the Chaldeans render תחמס! For all the lexicographers, relying on the etymology of the word, hold that it signifies a bird of prey. For חטף means to seize. Therefore חטפיתא, plainly derived from it, was believed to be a bird of the class τῶν γαμψωνύχων [tōn gampsōnychōn]; this is a very grave error. For the Chaldeans' חטפיתא chatphitha, or חטופיתא chatophitha, is the very same as the Arabs' خطاف [khuṭṭāf] chottaph, since in both the so-called radical letters are the same. Accordingly, in this very passage, for the Chaldee חטפיתא the Arabs have خطاف [khuṭṭāf] chottaph in three different paraphrases, of which two are printed and the third is in manuscript. Further, that the Arabic خطاف [khuṭṭāf] chottaph, whose plural is خطاطيف [khaṭāṭīf] chatatiph, is the swallow is clear from Avicenna and Abenbitar. They cite the passage of Dioscorides on the swallow near the end of his second book, Χελιδόνος νεοσσοὺς τοὺς ἐκ τῆς πρώτης νεοσσοποιΐας αὐξομένης τῆς Σελήνης ἀνατεμὼν, εὑρήσεις ἐν τῇ γαστρὶ λίθους [Chelidonos neossous tous ek tēs prōtēs neossopoiias auxomenēs tēs Selēnēs anatemōn, heurēseis en tē gastri lithous], etc., in Arabic thus, in the chapter خطاف [khuṭṭāf] cottaph: قال ديسقوريدوس [II, 835] في الثاني اذا اخذ فرخه في زيادة القمر وكان اول ما افرخ وشق وجد فيه حصايان [qāla Dīsqūrīdūs fī al-thānī idhā ukhidha farkhuhu fī ziyādat al-qamar wa-kāna awwal mā afrakha wa-shuqqa wujida fīhi ḥaṣāyān] Dioscorides said in the second book: if its chick is taken while the moon is waxing, and is from the first brood, and is cut open, stones are found in it, etc. Or واخذ من الحصا الموجودة في جوفه حصاتان [wa-ukhidha min al-ḥaṣā al-mawjūda fī jawfihi ḥaṣātān] And let two stones be taken from the stones that are found in its belly, etc., as Abenbitar has it. See the rest there, for there is no time to copy out more. Moreover Avicenna, in book 2, in the chapter خاليدونيون [khālīdūniyūn] Χελιδόνιον [Chelidonion], that is, swallow-wort, has among other things the following: اذا عمي فرخ لخطاطيف حملت اليه الام هذه النبات فزيده [col. 236] بصرا وكذلك سمي الخطافي [idhā ʿamiya farkh li-khaṭāṭīf ḥamalat ilayhi al-umm hādhihi al-nabāt fa-zīduhu baṣaran wa-kadhālika summiya al-khuṭṭāfī] When a chick of the chatatiph (swallows) is blinded, the mother brings it this plant, which increases its sight; hence it is called chottaphi (swallow-wort). And Abenbitar, in the chapter عروق الصباغين [ʿurūq al-ṣabbāghīn] dyers' roots, says that it is otherwise called بقلة الخطاطيف [baqlat al-khaṭāṭīf] herb of the chatatiph, or of the swallows. In the same place both chapters of Dioscorides on the greater and lesser celandine are given in Arabic. And his Greek words Ἐάν τις τυφλωθῇ τῶν τῆς χελιδόνος νεοσσῶν [Ean tis typhlōthē tōn tēs chelidonos neossōn] are rendered thus: اذا عمي فرخ من افراخ الخطاف [idhā ʿamiya farkh min afrākh al-khuṭṭāf] When some chick among the chicks of the alchottaph is blinded. The aspis chelidonias too is called خطاف [khuṭṭāf] chottaph by Avicenna, book 4 of the Canon, Fen 6, tract. 3, ch. 24. There is also the swallow fish, which Abuchalid Andalusius, or the Spaniard, describes under the name chottaph thus: الخطاف سمكة ببحر سبتة لها جناحان علي ظهرها اسودان وبها تخرج من الما وتطير الي الشجر ثم تعود الي البحر [al-khuṭṭāf samaka bi-baḥr Sabta lahā janāḥān ʿalī ẓahrihā aswadān wa-bihā takhruju min al-mā wa-taṭīru ilā al-shajar thumma taʿūdu ilā al-baḥr] The chottaph (or swallow) is a fish in the sea of Ceuta (near the Strait of Gades), furnished with two black wings on its back, with which it comes out of the sea and flies over the trees, and then returns to the sea. But nothing proves that خطاف [khuṭṭāf] is the swallow so much as its ample descriptions in Damir and Alkazuinius, from which we quoted some passages in the first book On Birds.
